analysis.one_liner: Makes the federal advisory committee that shapes railroad safety rules a permanent legal requirement.
analysis.headline: A railroad safety advisory committee bill from a single Ohio Democrat sits in a House subcommittee with zero cosponsors and no action since early February.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill writes the Railroad Safety Advisory Committee into federal law. That committee — made up of freight and passenger railroads, Amtrak, rail unions, local government groups, and rail suppliers — advises the Federal Railroad Administration on how it writes and updates railroad safety rules. Under the bill, the agency would be required by statute to keep the committee, meet with it quarterly, and report its work to Congress each year, with funding authorized from the Highway Trust Fund. Writing the committee into law means a future administration could not quietly shut it down; today it exists only at the agency's discretion. The bill has gone no further than a referral to a House subcommittee, and no other member of Congress has signed on.
analysis.who_benefits: Rail workers and people who live and work near rail lines, indirectly, if the committee keeps producing safety rules that an administration cannot dissolve. Rail labor unions gain a permanent, legally guaranteed seat at the rulemaking table, alongside railroads, Amtrak, and local governments. The Federal Railroad Administration gains a fixed structure for developing safety rules.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the Federal Railroad Administration to maintain the Railroad Safety Advisory Committee and sets its purpose as advising the Administrator on developing railroad safety regulatory programs, including new rules and revisions to existing ones.

The committee's membership must include at least one representative from each major stakeholder group, including freight and passenger railroads, Amtrak, local government organizations, rail passenger organizations, railroad labor unions representing operating, maintenance-of-way, shop and mechanical, clerks, and dispatching crafts, safety-related employees, and suppliers and manufacturers.
The agency must meet with the committee quarterly to consult on regulatory programs and receive its recommendations, and the committee must send Congress an annual report on its activities.

Codifying the committee in statute, with an exemption from the federal law that terminates advisory committees, makes it far harder for a future administration to eliminate it by administrative action.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the committee's operations — the bill authorizes whatever sums are necessary from the Highway Trust Fund, the account fed by federal gas taxes and highway-user fees. Freight railroads and rail suppliers bear indirect costs if the collaborative process produces stricter safety rules, and they also give up some unilateral influence because unions, passenger groups, and local governments hold guaranteed seats.
analysis.who_pays_short: Highway trust fund taxpayers and railroads

drawbacks.text: The committee only advises. It has no power to issue or block a rule; the Administrator is required to consult and receive recommendations, but can disregard them entirely, so the bill adds no new enforceable safety protection.

The bill locks in a consensus rulemaking process in which the regulated railroads and suppliers sit at the same table as unions and safety advocates, and consensus is generally reached only at the level of the slowest or most resistant participant — a structure that can soften or delay safety standards compared with the agency writing rules on its own.
Funding is authorized from the Highway Trust Fund, an account supported by federal gas taxes and highway-user fees, diverting highway-derived money to railroad administration work.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are real but modest. Making an advisory committee permanent protects a forum for rail safety rulemaking and guarantees labor and community interests a seat, at a small fiscal cost and a risk that consensus rulemaking slows down standards. Because the committee cannot force any rule, the bill's practical value depends entirely on future administrations and agency leaders choosing to use it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, which passed it to its railroads subcommittee, where nothing has happened since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on February 3, 2026, and referred to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
The next day, February 4, 2026, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials, where it has remained with no further action.
The bill has no cosponsors — not one other member of either party has signed onto it.
No hearing, markup, or vote of any kind has taken place.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won anything yet. The existing arrangement — an advisory committee that exists at the agency's discretion and can be altered or eliminated by an administration — continues unchanged, which leaves whoever prefers that flexibility better off for now.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; the bill sits untouched

for.name: Rep. Emilia Strong Sykes
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: No partisan pattern is visible: the bill has a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, and no committee or floor votes have occurred.

industries.note: The bill locks in a permanent seat for freight railroads on the committee that shapes the safety rules governing them, giving the industry a formal, statutorily guaranteed say. Consensus rulemaking can soften standards, but the guarantee also keeps a multi-party forum open that an administration could otherwise shut down.

Unions representing operating, maintenance-of-way, shop and mechanical, clerks, and dispatching crafts get a statutorily guaranteed seat on the safety rulemaking body, which they currently hold only at the agency's discretion.

Suppliers get a permanent seat helping shape safety standards that apply to their equipment, an interest that can cut against the strongest possible rules while also anchoring the process against elimination.
Amtrak and passenger rail groups are guaranteed representation in the development of railroad safety regulatory programs.

analysis.trajectory: Bills introduced by a single sponsor with no cosponsors and referred only to a subcommittee rarely reach the floor. Unless the subcommittee holds a hearing, the full committee acts, or the provisions get folded into a larger rail or transportation bill, the measure will most likely sit until the Congress ends in January 2027.
